script_body: For well over two millennia, humans have told one another stories about the danger of looking back at evil or death. Lot's wife turned to a pillar of salt for glancing over her shoulder into the maw of destruction; Orpheus lost his beloved forever for turning around before he reached the realm of light. And in a case of real life imitating those iconic tales, on September 11, 2001, the people on the streets around the Twin Towers when they fell had to run for their lives from the deadly debris cloud that pursued them with unrelenting fury. "Don't look back, just run," one bystander yells to another in one of the many moving videos preserved here.
key_claims: On September 11, 2001 people fled the debris cloud when the Twin Towers fell
A bystander video at the museum records 'Don't look back, just run'
source_passage: For well over 2 millennia, humans have been telling one another stories of the dangers of looking back at evil or death. Lot's wife turned to a pillar of salt because she dared glance over her shoulder into the maw of destruction. Orpheus lost his beloved forever for the same reason: He turned around before he'd reached the realm of light. And in a case of real life imitating iconic tales, on September 11, 2001, those people who were on the streets surrounding the Twin Towers when they fell had to run for their lives to escape the deadly debris cloud that pursued them with unrelenting fury. "Don't look back, just run," one bystander yells to another in one of the many moving videos at the 9/11 Memorial and Museum.

fact_check.notes: 9/11 date and Twin Towers collapse are established history; mythological allusions are the author's framing.

script_body: After a thorough security check, visitors descend down, down, down into this underground museum. It's a fitting metaphor: for the escape route Twin Towers survivors took when fleeing by stair — a remnant of the famous "survivors' stair" sits to the right of the museum's staircase — and for the darkness the attacks plunged the country into. At the bottom of the final staircase, to the left (oddly, as most visitors want to turn right), is the museum's beating heart, its history exhibition. A masterful mix of video, survivor audio, wall text, and poignant artifacts — the burnt-edged papers that fluttered from the Towers, children's clothing recovered from Flight 93 — brings the personal stories to life while explaining the forces that led to the attacks.

source_passage: After a thorough security check (make sure you allot 15 min. minimum for that and the entry line), visitors descend down, down, down into this underground museum. It's a fitting metaphor not only for the escape route that Twin Towers survivors had to take when fleeing by stair (a remnant of the famous "survivors stair" is to the right of the museum's staircase at one point) but also for the darkness the attacks plunged the United States into. At the bottom of the final staircase, to the left (oddly, as most visitors want to turn right) is the museum's beating heart: its history exhibition. A masterful mix of video, audio clips from survivors, wall text, and poignant artifacts—the burnt-edged papers that fluttered from the Towers, children's clothing recovered from Flight 93—the exhibit manages to bring to life the personal stories of those who lived or died that day, while also explaining some of the forces that led to the attacks.

The Memorial Room tells the story and shows the face of every person who died on 9/11.

script_body: Surrounding the museum is the eight-acre Memorial Plaza, with two reflecting pools and waterfalls set in the one-acre footprints of the individual towers. Each pool is ringed by a brass parapet engraved with the names of victims of both the 9/11 and the February 1993 bombings — arranged not alphabetically but according to where the victims worked, close to their co-workers and friends, or wherever their families felt they belonged.

script_body: Some fifteen thousand enslaved Africans were buried in a Manhattan graveyard during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, but their resting places were lost to memory — until 1991, when construction workers stumbled on human remains while renovating a federal building. The site is now considered one of the most important archaeological finds in the United States. In 2006 a handsome, symbol-laden National Monument, operated by the National Park Service, was dedicated here by poet Maya Angelou and Mayor Michael Bloomberg.

script_body: It took seven years and massive heartbreak to build the bridge's two great Gothic towers. In 1869, just two weeks after the project was approved, architect and immigrant John A. Roebling was surveying the area when a ferry rammed the spot where he stood, crushing his foot; he died of lockjaw three weeks later. His son Washington took over and devised pneumatic caissons — large, pressurized pine boxes pumped full of compressed air to keep the water out — that let six workers at a time descend to the riverbed to lay the foundations. Because no one yet understood underwater pressure, which scuba divers call "the bends," many workers were killed or injured, including Washington himself, who in 1872 had to be carried out partially paralyzed and remained an invalid for life. His wife Emily took over directing the job, learning advanced mathematics in the process, while Washington watched through binoculars from his apartment.

source_passage: It took 7 years and massive heartbreak to build these two structures. When architect (and immigrant) John A. Roebling was surveying the area in 1869, just 2 weeks after the project had been approved, a ferry accidentally rammed into the place where he was standing, crushing his foot. He died of lockjaw 3 weeks later. His son Washington took over and created a method of sending pneumatic caissons—basically large, pressurized pine boxes into which compressed air was pumped to keep the water out—down to the riverbed. This allowed six workers at a time to descend and lay the foundation for these towers. Because they didn't have a good understanding of the effects of underwater pressure on the human body (known to scuba divers as "the bends"), many were killed or injured in the caissons, including Washington Roebling. In 1872, he had to be carried out of the chamber, partially paralyzed. He remained an invalid for the rest of his life, and his wife Martha took over directing the job, learning advanced mathematics in the process. Washington watched the progress of the bridge through binoculars from his apartment...

script_body: From the center of the bridge, take in the views of both boroughs. When it was built, the span — 1,595 feet — was the longest leap across open space anywhere on Earth, and the first bridge to connect Manhattan with any of the surrounding lands. Look up at the cables: these too were an innovation, the first steel cables ever used on a bridge, where before then cables were iron. It took two years just to string them back and forth before the suspension work could begin. Each cable contains 5,434 wires and weighs 870 tons.

When the bridge was built, its span—1,595 feet—was the longest leap across an open space of any on Earth, and the first bridge to connect Manhattan with any of the lands that surrounded it. Take a look up at the cables; these, too, were an innovation, the first steel cables to be used on a bridge (before then cables were iron). It took 2 years to string the cables back and forth before work could begin building the suspension bridge. The cables each contain 5,434 wires and weigh 870 tons.

poi_name: Ellis Island National Museum of Immigration
script_body: Ellis Island was the epicenter of the largest migration in human history. From 1892 to 1954 it was in near-continuous use as the point-of-entry processing center for the majority of immigrants who settled in the United States in those years. Over twelve million people passed through its halls — sometimes as many as twelve thousand in a single day. What they were escaping, what they found, and what they endured during their short time in this purgatory of an island form the core of the Ellis Island experience.
key_claims: Ellis Island operated 1892–1954 as the main immigrant processing center

source_passage: The epicenter of the largest migration in human history, Ellis Island was in near-continuous use from 1892 to 1954 as the point-of-entry processing center for the majority of immigrants (including my grandmother) who settled in the U.S. during those years. Over 12 million people passed through its halls, sometimes as many as 12,000 in a single day. The stories of these immigrants—what they were escaping, what they found once here, and what they experienced in their short time in the purgatory that was Ellis Island—are the core of the Ellis Island experience.

fact_check.notes: 1892–1954 operation and ~12 million figure confirmed by Wikipedia, History.com, NPS.

poi_name: Ellis Island National Museum of Immigration
script_body: Begin on the awe-inspiring second-floor Grand Hall — officially the Registry Hall — beneath its massive white-tile vaulted ceiling, built by the same firm that made the ceiling in Grand Central's Oyster Bar. For most arrivals it was larger than any church or temple in their home village. Behind it lies a warren of small rooms where immigrants were tested for mental competency, literacy, and communicable disease. At listening stations you can hear actual immigrants recall the tests and the fear they inspired.

source_passage: Start in the awe-inspiring second-floor Grand Hall (officially the "Registry Hall"), with its massive white-tile vaulted ceiling (created by the same firm that did the ceiling in Grand Central Station's Oyster Bar; see p. 140), most likely larger than any church or temple these immigrants would have attended in their home villages. Behind the Grand Hall lies a warren of small rooms where immigrants were tested for mental competency, literacy, and communicable diseases. How these tests were done—and the fear they inspired—is chronicled in historical photos, wall text, and most poignantly at listening stations (or over the free audio-tour headphones) on which you hear actual immigrants share their memories of their time on the island.

script_body: The Hard Hat Tour leads through the unrenovated — and haunting — Ellis Island hospital. About ten percent of arriving immigrants spent time here, often only to be shipped back to Europe, their only crime being ill. The facility was closed for sixty years and is falling apart, hence the hard hats. The only new additions are oversize archival photos of hospital residents that French artist JR mounted onto the crumbling walls, broken windows, and metal lockers — a moving tribute.

poi_name: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
script_body: Descend eighty feet to the basement of this financial fortress and you'll see more lucre than you ever will again in your life. Behind a door a good five feet thick sits a gold vault straight out of Mission: Impossible, holding a full twenty-five percent of all the gold reserves in the world — far more than is kept in Fort Knox. Ninety-five percent of it belongs to foreign nations, who use this facility because, embedded in the bedrock of Manhattan and guarded by a small army of marksmen with their own on-site firing range, it's considered the safest place in the world for such storage. Currency hasn't been printed here since that function moved to New Jersey in 1992.

Down here, behind a door that's a good 5 feet thick, the Fed keeps $100,000 billion worth of gold bars, a full 25% of all the gold reserves in the world, far more than is kept in Fort Knox. Ninety-five percent of the gold stored here belongs to foreign nations, who use this facility, embedded in the bedrock of Manhattan and guarded by a small army of marksmen (they have their own on-site firing range for practice), because it's considered the safest place in the world for this type of storage.

script_body: Since a recent overhaul, this Holocaust memorial museum focuses far more on the personal stories of those whose lives were upended or ended — and on those who survived against all odds — told through thousands of personal accounts, never-before-seen photos, and striking artifacts. Among them: a breadloaf-size suitcase that one family of four escaped to freedom with, and, more chilling, an annotated edition of Mein Kampf that belonged to Heinrich Himmler. A 2023 exhibit, "The Danish Escape," tells the largely hopeful story of how the Danes saved much of their Jewish population.

script_body: Part of the allure of the view from the Western Hemisphere's tallest building, at 1,776 feet, is the sense that you may be tempting fate by being here. The skyscraper was built as a nose-thumb to the terrorists who twice attacked the World Trade Center on this same acre of ground. That defiance is brought home in a part of the lobby that shows the tunnel developers dug into the bedrock and kept purposefully rough-hewn, filled with lit signs about the durability of the rock and the fact that the building holds 5.4 million cubic feet of concrete — "making this the strongest building ever constructed."

script_body: Most visitors — and even some New Yorkers — don't know that the Staten Island Ferry makes its daily run within Instagram distance of the Statue of Liberty, Ellis Island, and Governor's Island, and riders pay absolutely nothing for the great views. Wait for one of the older orange-and-green boats, since the newer ones don't have viewing decks, and sit on the right side toward the back for the best look at the Manhattan skyline. Locals joke it's the best "cheap date" in the city — so don't be shy about toting along bread, cheese, and a bottle of wine.

script_body: The statue was dreamed up at a dinner party of French intellectuals in 1865, first proposed as a hundredth-birthday present from France to the United States — and as a not-so-subtle jab at France's own authoritarian Second Empire. Fundraising woes kept it from being finished in time for that anniversary, but after more than a decade of begging for money — a lottery finally did the trick — sculptor Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi completed the massive work in 1881.

script_body: Though the statue was finished, it took another two years for Americans to hold up their half of the bargain and build a pedestal. Newspaperman Joseph Pulitzer finally stepped in, and through a series of angry editorials condemning the wealthy for not contributing, he convinced thousands of lower-income Americans to send in what they could. Thanks to their dimes and nickels the pedestal — designed by Richard Morris Hunt — was at last built, and the statue was dedicated on October 28, 1886.

On the way up you'll see the intricate metalwork French engineer Gustave Eiffel, of Eiffel Tower fame, created to anchor the statue. It acts like a spring, letting the statue's "skin" adjust to changing temperatures and sway up to three inches in fifty-mile-per-hour winds.

script_body: Lady Liberty was created using repoussé, a technique of hammering and shaping thin strips of copper. Though the statue is massive — over 151 feet from base to torch — the "skin" is just three thirty-seconds of an inch thick. It's thought the ancient Colossus of Rhodes was built the same way. Every detail carries meaning: the seven rays in the crown stand for the seven seas, the 25 windows nod to 25 gemstones found on Earth, and the tablet bears the Roman numerals for July 4, 1776.

script_body: Built in 1766, St. Paul's is not only the oldest church in the city but the only public space in continuous use since the colonial era, its design — Ionic columns and a huge pediment — based on St. Martin-in-the-Fields in London. The chapel is redolent with history: George Washington kept a pew here, now marked by a plaque, and came straight to the church after his inauguration at nearby Federal Hall to pray and give thanks. On 9/11 it miraculously survived the rain of fiery metal when the Twin Towers fell, then became a focal point for the volunteer relief effort, where hundreds came from all over the world to search for survivors and remains, many sleeping and taking meals inside.

George Washington had a pew here (now marked by a plaque), and he came directly to the church after his inauguration at nearby Federal Hall (p. 312) to pray and give thanks. On 9/11, the church miraculously survived a rain of fiery metal when the Twin Towers collapsed, then served as a focal point for the volunteer effort that ensued, as hundreds of people came from all over the world to search for survivors and then human remains. Many slept at St. Paul's and took meals here (an exhibit in the church details this history).

script_body: This is actually the third Trinity Church on the site. The first was destroyed in the fire set by fleeing colonists in 1776 to thwart British occupiers — a blaze that razed a third of Manhattan's structures — and the second was so poorly built its roof collapsed in a snowstorm. The third, consecrated in 1846 and designed by Richard Upjohn, is considered by many the finest Gothic Revival building in the United States. Upjohn used self-consciously medieval features to underscore the sacred, even raising the chancel a few feet rather than railing it off, since formal barriers were controversial in Democratic New York. Among its Gothic features: stained glass, flying buttresses, and a 280-foot spire that was the tallest structure in the city until the Brooklyn Bridge's piers rose.

source_passage: This is actually the third Trinity Church to stand on this site. The first version was destroyed in the fire set by fleeing colonists in 1776 to thwart British occupiers (the fire ended up razing one-third of the structures in Manhattan). The second church building was poorly constructed, and its roof collapsed in a heavy snowstorm. But the third, consecrated in 1846, was a keeper and is considered by many to be one of the best, if not the best, Gothic Revival buildings in the United States. Designed by Richard Upjohn... Other Gothic features include lovely stained-glass windows, flying buttresses, and a towering 280-foot spire, which was the tallest structure in the city until the piers of the Brooklyn Bridge were built.

fact_check.notes: Third church, 1846 consecration, Richard Upjohn, Gothic Revival, and ~280/281-foot spire confirmed by NY Landmarks Conservancy and Wikipedia. 'Best in US' is a superlative opinion, kept attributed ('considered by many').

On the southern side, Captain James Lawrence — who gave the famous War of 1812 command "Don't give up the ship" — lies in a tomb shaped like a ship, ringed by a fence made from captured British cannons. Behind him and a little to the right is the cemetery's most famous grave, that of Alexander Hamilton, and beside Hamilton rests steamboat designer Robert Fulton.

script_body: In front of the Stock Exchange stands a scraggly buttonwood tree, planted to invoke the buttonwood under which New York's first traders gathered in 1792 to begin brokering Revolutionary War debt — the first stock market in America. One odd fact: though the NYSE is forever linked in the popular imagination with Wall Street, its facade actually fronts Broad Street, not Wall. The exchange no longer offers public tours, but you can grab a coffee and "toast" the brokers in nearby Zuccotti Park, birthplace of the Occupy Wall Street movement.

script_body: This soaring "Cathedral of Commerce" cost Frank W. Woolworth fourteen million dollars' worth of nickels and dimes in 1913. It was the tallest building in the city from 1913 until 1930, when the Chrysler Building surpassed it. At its opening, President Woodrow Wilson pressed a button from the White House that lit the building's 80,000 electric bulbs. Critic Paul Goldberger called it the "Mozart of skyscrapers" — its neo-Gothic exterior festooned with spires, gargoyles, flying buttresses, castlelike turrets, and stone-as-lace traceries above a churchlike interior.

script_body: Housed in an 1887 synagogue — the oldest house of worship in the city built by Eastern European Jews — the Museum at Eldridge Street has the kind of grandeur usually reserved for the cathedrals of Europe. There's poignancy here too: the building was abandoned for forty years before restoration began in the 1990s, and in places it's still crumbling picturesquely away. The "From Bottom to Top" tour, offered on the hour, traces the synagogue's history and the challenges of its restoration.

script_body: At first glance this museum looks like just another brownstone on the block — and that's exactly the point. It was the first National Trust for Historic Preservation site that wasn't the home of someone rich or famous; its original building at 97 Orchard Street was preserved to tell the story of the immigrants who lived within. Those stories are rich and varied: this five-story tenement housed some 10,000 people from 25 countries between 1863 and 1935. In 2017 the museum added a second building, 103 Orchard, to tell the stories of more recent immigrants.

In 2017, the museum added another building (103 Orchard) to tell the stories of more recent immigrants to the United States.

script_body: On East 4th Street this precious sliver of history has survived utterly intact — the only Victorian-era structure in New York City preserved both inside and out. A handsome Greek Revival town house, it was once home to the Tredwell family, who furnished it in the highest style of the day: silk-upholstered couches, bronze gas chandeliers, deep burgundy curtains. Those furnishings, the ten-person family's clothing and cookware, and much more are all on display, thanks to the 1936 efforts of a preservationist — before there really was such a thing — named George Chapman. A lovely garden and frequent ghost sightings add to the home's appeal.

script_body: Found objects in a found space — that, in a nutshell, is what makes this nutshell-size gallery so beguiling. Set in a non-working, sixty-square-foot freight elevator shaft off an alley, it was created by three indie filmmakers drawn to objects that illuminate the world around them. The permanent collection includes a compass that points toward Mecca for prayer, a snow globe from North Korea, and a prison-issued fingertip toothbrush. Changing exhibits run from the oddball — weirdly shaped cornflakes — to the poignant, like a collection of "last text messages" sent just before someone died or cut off communication.

script_body: The story of the Chinese immigrant experience in the U.S. is unlike that of any other ethnic group. Arguably these Chinese Americans, like the African Americans brought here as slaves, faced a far harder road than other immigrants — held to limited work and then barred outright by the "Chinese Exclusion Act," a federal law that halted further Chinese immigration and separated countless families. That history gives this small museum, designed by Maya Lin — creator of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington — its true power. In 2020 a fire gutted the museum's storage facility, but grants and hard work may have it back to full operation.

For a preview, go to www.mocanyc.org/visit to look at Maya Lin's video tour of the museum (she's the museum's designer as well as the creator of the Vietnam Veteran's Memorial in Washington, D.C.). Sadly, the museum's storage facility was gutted by a fire in 2020...

script_body: In May 2015 the Whitney's new Renzo Piano–designed home opened in the Meatpacking District, right next to the High Line park. The design is built for flexibility: floors can be drilled into, every interior wall is movable, and every inch is wired for electronic art. It's also unusually kind to visitors — many rooms flooded with natural light, floors sprung on "sleepers" so there's no foot fatigue, and the museum is 60 percent larger than its old Upper East Side home, so the best-known pieces of its permanent collection — Calder's "Circus," Hopper's bleak beauties, O'Keeffe's blossoms — can stay on display on the fifth and sixth floors.

script_body: Look out at the river. It's the reason this great city was built. When Henry Hudson and his crew of sixteen sailed up it in 1609, mistakenly thinking they'd find Asia at its mouth, little did they know they were setting in motion a chain of events that would still be shaping lives over four hundred years later. Hudson's reports about the trading possibilities of the area — particularly for valuable animal pelts — plus his amazement at the great natural harbor here, spurred the Dutch to create settlements. They guessed, rightly, that the harbor of New York would be the linchpin connecting Europe, via the Atlantic, with the interior of this vast and wealthy continent, via the Hudson River. Later, after the building of the Erie Canal, which connected the Hudson with the Great Lakes, New York became the most powerful city in the nation.

script_body: This circular stone structure — taller in some earlier incarnations — has been at the center of New York life over the years. In 1807, the West Battery, as it was then called, was built as a fort on a landfill island in the water off Manhattan, to ward off British invasions. It never saw action, however: during the War of 1812 the British attacked Washington, D.C., instead. script_body: In 1855, the space was transformed once more, into the city's first immigrant processing center. Over eight million new arrivals — a full two-thirds of those who came to the United States at this time — spent their first hours in the country here, registering their names with the government, exchanging money, and getting information on jobs, medical care, and lodgings. By 1890, the vast number of immigrants, and the growing problem of outsiders scamming them, necessitated a move to a larger and more easily patrolled offshore space: Ellis Island, which you can see from here, to the right of the Statue of Liberty, its main hall reaching into the sky with four little spires.

script_body: At the base of this flagpole is a bas-relief sculpture depicting the historic scene of Dutch official Peter Minuit 'buying' Manhattan from Native American residents in 1626, to consolidate the Dutch colony in one easily defended spot. Just how the 'sale' went down is still a matter of controversy. Most likely the 'sellers' were the Canarsie tribe who, according to a letter by Dutch merchant Peter Schagen, let the island go for sixty guilders — the equivalent of twenty-four dollars. But did the Indians know they were selling the island, or did they think they were simply accepting shiny trinkets as part of a welcome ceremony? And were the Canarsie even in a position to sell it, as it had long been a communal hunting ground used by a number of tribes? We'll never know the truth, but this is the one place in Manhattan where the most infamous real estate deal in history is memorialized.

script_body: You are now standing at the foot of Broadway, the thoroughfare that leads all the way to the top of Manhattan, thirteen miles away. The original Dutch fort stood in this exact place. The building in front of you, designed by Cass Gilbert, was one of the most important structures in the city when it was built — the Alexander Hamilton U.S. Customs House. Before 1913, when the federal government instituted the personal income tax, the government's revenue came almost entirely from customs on imported goods. A full seventy-five percent of that revenue came from the Port of New York, processed in this grand Beaux Arts colossus, completed in 1907 and comprising over four hundred and fifty thousand square feet of interior space.

script_body: It's a wedding cake of an edifice, with dozens of bright white sculptures adorning the gray granite facade. Daniel Chester French was the sculptor — he also did the seated Lincoln at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C. — and his choice of symbols could be read as a treatise on the prejudices of Victorian-era America. The four seated women at the front represent the four 'great' continents. From left to right, they are Asia; the Americas, with South America barely present, tellingly represented by the Aztec-like structure that North America has her foot on; Europe; and Africa. America and Europe look full of vigor and purpose, but Asia has her eyes closed, perhaps in meditation, and Africa — in a metaphor for her supposed lack of vision and power — is in a deep slumber. America shelters a new immigrant crouching to her left, pushing forward a winged wheel, those of the Roman god Mercury, divine overseer of commerce.

script_body: On July 9, 1776, the Declaration of Independence was read aloud near City Hall, and a small battalion of agitated colonists marched here to behead the statue of King George that stood in the center of the park. It had been erected just five years earlier by many of these same men, in gratitude for the king's part in repealing the odious Stamp Act — the one that provoked the 'no taxation without representation' movement. Though it can't be proven, legend has it that the lead statue was then melted down and used for cannon balls and bullets in the war against the British. The fence that rings the park is the original, one of the few colonial structures of any sort left in Manhattan; when first erected, its spokes had royal crowns at their tips, and these too were destroyed by the colonists.

script_body: Here you'll have a remarkably accurate snapshot of what the city looked like around 1837. This narrow, winding street was the first to be paved in New Amsterdam and the only one thought to still sit where the Dutch colonists originally placed it. All of the buildings went up immediately after the great fire of 1835, which devastated the city, wiping out twenty square blocks. Many blamed the volunteer firefighters of the time who, working in rival squads for cash payment, spent more time fighting one another than the flames — a battle Martin Scorsese's 2002 film Gangs of New York dramatically re-creates.

script_body: Mill Lane has the distinction of being the shortest street on Manhattan — and yes, there was once a mill here. Folk tradition held that it was here that Peter Stuyvesant, the Dutch Director-General of New Amsterdam, signed a treaty of surrender when the British invaded. Thanks to recently uncovered documents, we now know that act actually happened at Stuyvesant's farm, in what is today the East Village. Stuyvesant surrendered unwillingly, having torn to pieces the first letter sent by the British warship commander. City leaders then painstakingly pieced the letter back together; upon seeing its favorable terms — colonists could keep their land and businesses — ninety-three leading citizens, including Stuyvesant's seventeen-year-old son, demanded he surrender the colony. Stuyvesant did so but mourned the loss for the rest of his life.

source_passage: Mill Lane has the distinction of being the shortest street on Manhattan (and yes, there was once a mill here). Folk tradition had it that it was here that Peter Stuyvesant, the Dutch Director-General of New Amsterdam, signed a treaty of surrender when the British invaded. Thanks to recently uncovered documents, we know that historic act actually happened at Stuyvesant's farm, in what is today the East Village. Stuyvesant surrendered unwillingly, having torn to pieces the first letter sent by the British warship commander. City leaders then pieced the letter painstakingly back together. Upon seeing the favorable terms it presented the colonists (they would be allowed to keep their land and businesses), 93 leading citizens—including Stuyvesant's 17-year-old son, a traitorous young fogey—demanded Stuyvesant surrender the colony to the British. Stuyvesant did so but mourned the loss of the colony for the rest of his life.

script_body: Here is New York's greatest monument to thwarted ambition. Architect H. Craig Severance dreamed of building the tallest building in the world, taller than the Woolworth Building, which had held the record from 1917 to 1930. The trouble was that his former partner and archrival William Van Alen had the same aspiration. In the summer of 1929, at the height of the bubble before Black Tuesday, they began a 'race to the top' — Severance at 40 Wall Street, Van Alen at the Chrysler Building. In a record eleven months, Severance finished this building for the Bank of Manhattan, certain his structure would be the tallest. But Van Alen then administered the coup de grâce he'd hidden in his elevator shaft: the Chrysler Building's iconic Art Deco spire, which added an unbeatable hundred and twenty-five feet. The Chrysler's own title was snatched away just one year later by the Empire State Building.

Craig Severance had a dream: He wanted to build the tallest building in the world, taller than the Woolworth Building (which held the record from 1917–30). Problem was, his former partner and archrival William Van Alen had the same aspirations, and in the summer of 1929, at the height of the bubble that preceded Black Tuesday (the great stock market crash), they began a "race to the top," Severance at 40 Wall St. and Van Alen at the Chrysler Building (p. 208). script_body: Note the austere building across the street; it was the headquarters of banker J. P. Morgan — the window of his former office is above the flagpole. Look closely at the side facing Federal Hall and you'll see it is pocked with small indentations: the scars of the Financial District's first terrorist attack, in 1920. One bright, sunny morning, a horse and carriage loaded with explosives parked here. Moments later a huge explosion shook the street, killing thirty-one people and wounding scores more. The blast was so powerful that all that was ever found of the horse was a horseshoe. Police traced it to a blacksmith who vaguely recalled shoeing the horse of an Italian man, and on that scanty evidence the police and press decided the blast must have been the work of Italian anarchists. No one was ever charged.

script_body: Look down as you amble along Broadway at the brass plates naming the ticker-tape parades held along this stretch. Had you been here in the 1930s or '40s, the crowds would have stood shoulder-to-shoulder, and above your head hundreds at the windows would have showered the street with long paper ribbons of stock quotations spewing from their machines. Read the plates: the catalogue of names is a retread of American history and political alliances. Along with athletes, astronauts, and presidents, you'll find parades for the American hostages released from Iran in 1982, pianist Van Cliburn in 1958, and the controversial President Sukarno of Indonesia in 1956.

script_body: Touring Harlem takes imagination, because much of what made it unique during the fabled Jazz Era — the Harlem Renaissance — crumbled beneath the wrecking ball decades ago. The wide avenues, rows of brownstones, and elegant apartment buildings you see now are an accident of history: the physical face of an area that housed a people but wasn't necessarily 'of' that people. Despite all this, Harlem remains the African-American capital of the United States, sometimes called the 'capital for Africans throughout the world.' As architect Zevilla Jackson Preston writes in HarlemWorld, 'Ultimately it is the energy on the street, the beat on the street — all of the beautiful Black people on the streets — that make the experience unique.'

source_passage: The tragic fact is that much of what made this area unique, lively, and . . . well, Harlem, during the fabled Jazz Era (aka the Harlem Renaissance), crumbled beneath the wrecking ball decades ago. What you now see—wide avenues, rows of brownstones, elegant apartment buildings—are somewhat an accident of history, the physical face of an area that housed a people but wasn't necessarily “of” that people (I'll explain below). Despite all this, Harlem remains the African-American capital of the United States (sometimes called the “capital for Africans throughout the world”), a one-of-a-kind area with much to recommend it. Architect Zevilla Jackson Preston best sums up its appeal in the book HarlemWorld, in which she writes, “Ultimately it is the energy on the street, the beat on the street—all of the beautiful Black people on the streets—that make the experience unique.”

script_body: Harlem was settled in waves — Dutch farmers first, then their British counterparts, then poor Irish and Italian immigrants. But development only took off just before 1904, when the city's first subway line opened: a nine-and-a-half-mile snaking tunnel connecting Lower Manhattan with points as far north as 145th Street. In anticipation, an unprecedented housing boom hit the neighborhood, developers slapping up Victorian row house after row house for the crowds of upwardly mobile immigrants — middle-class Jews and Germans, primarily — they were certain would flood this newly commutable neighborhood. What they didn't anticipate were the recessions and panics of 1893, 1907, and 1910, which deflated the housing market and left them overbuilt.

source_passage: Harlem was settled by a number of different groups over the years— Dutch farmers first, followed by their British counterparts, then poor Irish and Italian immigrants. But development only took off in the years just prior to 1904, when the city's first subway line opened, a 91⁄2-mile snaking tunnel connecting Lower Manhattan with points as far north as 145th Street. In anticipation of this event, an unprecedented housing boom hit the neighborhood, with developers slapping up Victorian row house after row house for the crowds of upwardly mobile immigrants—middle-class Jews and Germans, primarily—they were certain would soon flood this newly commutable neighborhood. What they didn't anticipate were recessions and panics in 1893, 1907, and 1910, which deflated the housing market and badly affected the development of large numbers of homes on the Upper West Side.

script_body: Left with hundreds of unrentable homes, property owners began doing what nobody else had done in the history of the United States: renting or selling brand-new, beautifully appointed buildings to the race that had until then always made do with tumble-down ghetto housing no other group would accept. In 1905, pioneering real estate agent Philip Payton persuaded a white landlord to rent him 31 W. 133rd St. so he could re-lease it to African Americans — promising to pay a substantial $5 more per tenant per month, a lot of money in those days. Several other white landlords panicked and bought the building to evict the Black tenants, but by then it was too late: Payton had the funding to buy several other buildings, and Black migration into the area began in earnest.

source_passage: Left with hundreds of unrentable homes, property owners soon began doing what nobody else had done in the history of the United States: renting or selling brand-new, often beautifully appointed buildings to the race that had, until that point, always made do with the tumble-down ghetto housing no other group would accept. In 1905, pioneering real estate agent Philip Payton persuaded a white landlord to rent him 31 W. 133rd St. so he could re-lease it to African Americans. The landlord accepted the offer because Payton promised to pay far more than the going rate, a substantial $5 more per tenant per month (a lot of money in those days). Several other white landlords panicked and bought the building in order to evict the Black tenants, but by then it was too late. Payton had the funding to buy several other buildings, and Black migration into the area began in earnest.

script_body: In 1969, an act of kindness changed the lives of thousands of children. A young woman named Lorraine Hale was driving on 146th Street when she saw a drugged-out mother nodding off on the street, her two-month-old baby almost slipping from her arms. Ms. Hale got out, told the mother she needed treatment, and said she could leave the baby with her own mother — Clara McBride Hale — while she got sober. The next day the addicted mother did just that, and soon hundreds of babies were being left with 'Mother Hale,' who pioneered methods of treating babies born with addictions and also took in many HIV-positive babies.

It's the work of architect William Tuthill, who later went on to design Carnegie Hall. As in many Gotham brownstones, the main entrance is on the second floor, not the ground floor. Why? script_body: This park — long known as Mount Morris Park, named for General Roger Morris — was created in honor of the very first American victory in the Revolutionary War. It was near where you stand, on September 16, 1776, that George Washington engaged in what he called a 'brisk little skirmish' with the Redcoats. Just a month earlier the largest British expeditionary fleet in history had sailed into New York Harbor with 21,000 troops, a full 40% of all the men in the Royal Navy at the time. Those soldiers had slaughtered about 2,800 American militiamen at the Battle of Brooklyn, forcing Washington to flee Brooklyn by night to the northern reaches of Manhattan. Here, at the small battle called the Battle of Washington Heights, enemy buglers taunted the colonists by playing the call that traditionally ended a foxhunt. Enraged, Washington called for reinforcements and drove the Redcoats back to what is now the Upper West Side — the first time his soldiers had won an engagement, doing much to boost morale.

script_body: This pretty pocket park marks the site where the most famous hoarders of the pre-television age once lived: a pair of reclusive brothers who occupied their home here from the 1880s until their deaths in 1947. Rumors swirled about their compulsive behavior, but nobody knew the extent of it until both were found dead, surrounded by 140 tons of stuff — books, musical instruments, towering stacks of newspapers, baby carriages, guns, furniture, and all manner of junk, all rigged with booby traps to ward off outsiders. It took over a year to clear the house, which was eventually razed; it was rotting on its foundations.

script_body: This intersection is one of the most important in Harlem. Look first to the windswept northeast corner, where a statue of Adam Clayton Powell, Jr. — Harlem's first African-American congressman — stands. This is also the spot where Malcolm X spent many hours lecturing Harlem residents on behalf of the Nation of Islam. His message — 'We are Blacks first and everything else second' — was so powerful, and he such an effective orator, that before he left the NOI the organization had nearly half a million members; it dwindled rapidly after he resigned. His controversial message rejected non-violence and condemned integration as cultural suicide, going directly against the goals of the NAACP, the largest civil rights organization of the time.

script_body: Across the street rises the tall white building with geometric patterns climbing its facade — the former Hotel Theresa. In 1960 a young Fidel Castro was scheduled to address the United Nations, but no hotel in town would take him and his contingent. After he threatened to camp on the U.N. lawn, the government ordered city hotels to accommodate him, but Castro quarreled with the midtown Shelburne Hotel he'd chosen. After a conversation with Malcolm X, he moved up here to the Theresa — a gesture of solidarity with Black Americans. Clashes between pro- and anti-Castro forces kept the 258 police officers guarding him busy, and on his second day Nikita Khrushchev came to visit; the combined police contingents created the greatest show of force Harlem had ever witnessed, unmatched to this day.

script_body: When it opened in 1900, Blumstein's was the neighborhood's largest and most exclusive store, built at a cost of $1 million — note the beautifully worked copper ornamentation on the facade, a mix of Art Deco and Spanish Renaissance. It was owned by Louis Blumstein, the synagogue congregant from the tour's start. Although the vast majority of its clientele was African American, Blumstein's refused to hire any Black clerks — a maddening policy during the Great Depression. In 1934 the Urban League, spearheaded by Reverends John H. Johnson and Adam Clayton Powell, Jr., launched a boycott and picket of the store. For two months picketers carried signs reading 'Don't buy where you can't work.' Blumstein's finally relented, hiring 34 African-American women as clerks. Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. often cited this strike as an example of the power of non-violent protest.

script_body: In 1958, Dr. King himself was at the center of history at Blumstein's. He was seated at a table signing copies of his book Strides Towards Freedom when a Black woman named Izola Ware Curry reached the front of the line. After asking, 'Are you Martin Luther King?' she pulled a letter opener from the book she was carrying and, shouting 'You Communist, you Communist!', stabbed him in the chest. King was rushed to Harlem Hospital with the blade still in — had it been removed, he would have bled to death — and underwent surgery. The next morning the New York Times reported that had King sneezed, he would have died, as the blade was touching his aorta. From his hospital bed, King issued a letter of forgiveness to Curry, who was committed to an asylum; she had a long history of mental instability.

script_body: Greenwich Village started as its own village — a place where, as in Boccaccio's Decameron, the well-to-do fled on a near-yearly basis to escape the plagues of colonial Nieuw Amsterdam and then New York City, mostly recurrent bouts of yellow fever. Building began in earnest in the 1820s and 1830s, with wealthy families putting up row house after row house in what was then a suburb. Then the city caught up: the hoi polloi moved in just down the block, and the bluebloods did the 19th-century version of urban flight, decamping a mile uptown. Their swank houses were carved into cheap apartments and boarding houses, or torn down for factories, and the neighborhood filled with immigrants and, later, artists. It kept its status as a place apart thanks to its tangle of twisting, narrow streets — "The streets have run crazy and broken themselves," O. Henry wrote, "into strange angles and curves. One street crosses itself a time or two." In the 1960s and '70s that quiet charm drew the wealthy back, and it became a hideaway once more.

Building began in earnest in the 1820s and 1830s, with wealthy families building row house after row house in what was then a suburb. Soon, of course, the city caught up, the hoi polloi were living just down the block, and the bluebloods did the 19th-century version of urban flight and moved a mile uptown to newer suburbs. Their swank houses were subdivided into cheap apartments and boarding houses, or torn down entirely to create factories. The neighborhood became home to immigrants and later, artists. The Village always retained its status as a place apart, however, thanks to the confusing configuration of its streets, a jumble of twisting byways and narrow streets. "The streets have run crazy and broken themselves . . . into strange angles and curves," O. Henry wrote. "One street crosses itself a time or two." In the 1960s and '70s, the charm of this urban topography, the quiet of the tiny streets cut off from upper Manhattan's bustle, brought the well-to-do back, and the neighborhood became once more a hideaway for wealthy New Yorkers.

script_body: Hangings, protests, burials, parades — if another spot in New York has seen as much drama as Washington Square Park, the guidebook hadn't heard of it. North of the first Dutch settlement in Manhattan, this was originally marshland fed by a stream that still runs under nearby Minetta Lane. Its first settlers were Nieuw Amsterdam slaves who, in 1641, were given partial freedom in return for farming this then-dangerous, remote acreage. They were primarily older men and women who had outlived their usefulness to their masters, and their freedom was a mixed blessing: they had to hand over a large part of their harvests to the colony and, more disturbingly, they became human watchdogs, posted here to alert the Dutch if local Indians or British forces tried to attack.

script_body: In 1797 the drained swamp was designated a potter's field, and it was put to grim use a year later when yellow fever swept the city. Over five percent of New York's population died that muggy, mosquito-infested summer, and the poorest of them — nearly 20,000 people — were buried right here. In 1826 the ground became a military parade ground, and tales were told of soldiers drilling here, their boots slipping through the crust of the dirt and crunching down on shroud-covered skeletons. As if that weren't haunting enough, the square was often used for public hangings, the condemned strung up on a massive elm that still stands on the park's northwest corner.

script_body: The magnificent white marble arch at the foot of Fifth Avenue was designed by Stanford White — his second such arch. The first, made of wood and plaster, was erected in 1889 to mark the centennial of George Washington's inauguration and to raise funds for this permanent version, completed in 1892. Look to the right side of the arch: the sculpture there, Washington as President, Accompanied by Wisdom and Justice, was added in 1918 by Alexander Stirling Calder, father of the great modern mobile-maker Alexander Calder. On the other side, Washington as Commander-in-Chief, Accompanied by Fame and Valor, by Herman Atkins MacNeill, was tacked on the same year.

script_body: The arch has long been a choice target for protesters. In 1918, by Frommer's account, Dada daddy Marcel Duchamp climbed the 110 interior steps with fellow members of the Liberal Club — including a woman who called herself "Woe," so she could declaim "Woe is Me!" — carrying Chinese lanterns, food, wine, and cap guns, to declare Greenwich Village an "independent republic." An unamused constable soon brought them down. Less lighthearted was a 1968 takeover by the Students Against Racism and War, who barricaded themselves inside to hang a banner protesting the Vietnam War. The door to the inner stairway has been bolted ever since.

script_body: Dash-dot-dot-dash — you've reached the birthplace of the telegraph. Inventor Samuel Morse lived in this New York University building, where he was a painting instructor, when in 1836 he worked out the rudiments of the telegraphic alphabet better known as Morse Code. script_body: You're looking at the longest unbroken string of Greek Revival town houses anywhere in the United States. New York University owns most of them now — in fact it owns much of the neighborhood — but in the 1830s, when they were built, they were strictly for individual owners of the highest social class. The Greek Revival style was no accident. In the mid-1820s, support for the Greeks — a Christian nation fighting for independence from the Ottoman Empire — was all the rage among the upper echelons of Manhattan society. That enthusiasm, plus the notion that America was a modern version of ancient Greek democracy, is why classical columns started popping up on buildings all over town, with Greek symbols worked into fences, pedestals added to facades, and so on.

Henry James' grandmother lived here, and he used the area as inspiration for the famed novel Washington Square (later turned into the play and film The Heiress). script_body: On March 25, 1911, a horrific tragedy on this site reshaped New York State law and the history of the American labor movement. That Saturday, some 600 young women — mostly Jewish and Italian immigrants between 13 and 23 — were at work in a garment factory on the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors. At 5pm, just as they were getting ready to leave, a fire sprang up in the southeast corner of the eighth floor; no one has ever determined the cause. Within minutes all three floors were an inferno, and an inescapable one, because many doors had been locked from the outside — to prevent theft, the owners later said. A fire escape collapsed and the elevator operator fled, but a pedestrian named Joseph Zito ran in, got the elevator working, and made five trips up through the flames, saving 25 to 30 workers each time. Still, several young women jumped to their deaths in front of horrified passersby, others suffocated, and some were crushed at the locked doors. In all, 146 people were killed at the Triangle Shirt Waist Factory, most in the first ten minutes of the hour-long blaze.

source_passage: On March 25, 1911, a horrific tragedy on this site reshaped the laws of New York State and the history of the American labor movement. On that Saturday, some 600 young women, mostly Jewish and Italian immigrants between the ages of 13 and 23, were hard at work in a garment factory on the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors of this building. At 5pm, just as the workers were getting ready to leave, a fire sprung up in the southeast corner of the eighth floor—no one has ever been able to determine the cause—and within minutes all three floors were an inferno. An inescapable one, it turned out, because many of the doors had been locked from the outside (to prevent theft, the owners said later). Minutes after that, one of the fire escapes collapsed, and the elevator operator fled in terror. A brave pedestrian named Joseph Zito ran into the building, got the elevator working, and made five trips up through the flames, saving 25 to 30 workers on each trip. Fleeing the flames, several young women jumped to their deaths in front of horrified passersby. Those trapped inside suffocated from the smoke, while still others were crushed in a heap at the locked doors. In all, 146 people were killed at the Triangle Shirt Waist Factory, most within the first 10 minutes of the hour-long blaze.

script_body: The more theatrical strain of Greenwich Village bohemianism found its home at the little theater that once stood here — only the name remains — at one point one of the city's most influential playhouses. That was thanks largely to Eugene O'Neill, who managed it and whose important early works were first performed here, among them Emperor Jones, The Hairy Ape, and The Great God Brown. Overturning barriers, the theater cast African Americans to play African Americans, and even featured a kiss between a Black man and a white woman — a radical move in 1926, one that drew threats from the Ku Klux Klan.

script_body: In 1863, when the riots surrounding the Civil War's first draft lottery morphed into race riots, this was one of the few safe places in the city for Black Americans. For five days hundreds of white hooligans raged through the streets, beating and lynching Blacks and even burning down an orphanage for Black children — the most violent riot of the century, with 105 people killed and many more maimed for life. But the narrow layout of Minetta Street let armed residents successfully guard their homes and families from harm.

script_body: Attention Hamilton fans: in the 1790s the widowed Aaron Burr moved into this 1767 carriage house with his daughter Theodosia. After the tragic duel, Burr lost not only his political career but much of his property, including this building. It later became an engine house for the local firehouse, and in the 1890s a saloon and brothel. The restaurant here today is still a stop on ghost tours — many claim it's haunted by Aaron, Theodosia, and some of the ladies of the night who once worked here. The specters get blamed whenever a customer's earring goes missing.

script_body: Oddly enough, it was an organized-crime sting operation that precipitated the raid that gave birth to the contemporary gay rights movement. By the 1960s the Genovese crime family owned most gay bars in the Village, serving watered-down liquor to a community that had few other places to meet — and blackmailing wealthier customers with the threat of outing. The family usually paid off the police, but on June 28, 1969, the Stonewall wasn't tipped off. When eight officers showed up at 1:20am and began loading employees and customers into a police van, patrons started pelting them with pennies, cans, bottles, and bricks. The melee escalated, and thousands rioted for another five days before order was restored. While these protests weren't the start of the gay rights movement, many feel they were its galvanizing force — which is why pride celebrations in New York and worldwide now fall on the anniversary weekend of the riots.

source_passage: Oddly enough, it was an organized-crime sting operation that precipitated the raid that gave birth to the contemporary gay rights movement. By the 1960s, the Genovese crime family owned most gay bars in the Village, where they served watered-down liquor to a community that didn't have many other places to meet; they also blackmailed wealthier customers with the threat of outing. The family regularly paid off the police, but on June 28, 1969, the Stonewall wasn't tipped off in advance. When eight police officers showed up at 1:20am and started loading employees and customers into a police van, patrons began pelting them with pennies, cans, bottles, and bricks. As the melee escalated, thousands of people rioted for another 5 days before order could be restored. While these protests weren't the start of the gay rights movement, many feel that they were the galvanizing force. Today, pride celebrations in New York, and worldwide, take place on the anniversary weekend of the riots.

fact_check.notes: June 28, 1969 date, 1:20am raid, and organized-crime/Genovese ownership corroborated by Wikipedia, Britannica, History.com.

script_body: This is where New York City—then New Amsterdam—was born. The area packs the same historic punch as colonial sections of Boston and Philadelphia. It was on Wall Street that George Washington took the oath of office as America's first president, and it was here, at Fraunces Tavern, that the Sons of Liberty gathered to plot the overthrow of the British. At Castle Clinton and then Ellis Island, millions of immigrants flooded the city in the 19th and 20th centuries to get their first glimpse of a “promised land.”

script_body: For millions, this area was once the portal to America. The buildings you see on the Lower East Side were built expressly to house the teeming masses of immigrants who flooded into New York between roughly 1840 and 1930. At the turn of the last century, this was the most densely populated area in the world, with a dozen people to an apartment and pushcarts jamming the streets. Some remnants of that life survive in the old-world fabric and luggage stores along Orchard Street.

script_body: For 25 years, the non-profit Big Apple Greeter has paired volunteer New Yorkers with visitors for free, highly personal looks at the city. The guides aren't expected to spout history or architecture; instead they introduce tourists to the city they know and love, taking them to areas few outsiders see. The four-hour tours are for individuals and couples—the largest group accepted is five—and are so hugely popular that you should book four weeks in advance, because many would-be participants are turned away.

script_body: Greenwich Village has always been where the city's outsiders and oddballs found a haven. In Dutch Colonial times it was farmland set outside the walls of the city. At the turn of the 20th century it was a bohemian enclave where artists of all sorts—Mark Twain, Edgar Allan Poe, Eugene O'Neill, and Winslow Homer among them—could find cheap lodging and companionship. In the 1950s it sat at the center of the Beat movement; in the '60s and '70s the area around Christopher Street became the hub of a burgeoning gay rights movement; and in the '80s it was a hotbed of AIDS-related activism.

script_body: As you meander through these areas you're likely to see brown street signs proclaiming “Ladies Mile.” It was on this stretch, mostly on Broadway and Park Avenue South, that the first wave of department stores transformed the lives of New Yorkers in the 1850s. Instead of hopping from a dry-goods shop for fabric to a milliner for hats to a cobbler for shoes, women came from all over the city to outfit themselves and their homes in stores that had everything under one roof. Notice the large plate-glass windows on many facades, another department store innovation.

script_body: Midtown West encompasses several famous places: Madison Square Garden, the Garment District, Rockefeller Center, the Theater District, and Times Square. In just the past 50 years it’s gone from being a somewhat insulated community of Irish and Italian Americans to the most international community in the United States. A single afternoon in Queens can make a visitor feel like a globe-trotter, which gives Queens a special appeal, despite the dreary, industrial look of much of it. Whether you’re downing samosas or shopping for saris in very Indian Jackson Heights, breaking plates at a Greek restaurant in Astoria, or buying miracle water and tacos at a Mexican botanica in Corona, there’s much to taste, smell, and experience.

script_body: Finding your way around Manhattan is easier than in almost any other city because of the careful plan adopted for its avenues and streets. In the areas above 14th Street, the city fathers imposed a strict grid, leveling hills and tearing down existing homes to create straight, evenly spaced thoroughfares in all but a few places. The grid consists of numbered streets and avenues that cross at right angles—so if you can count to 100, you can get around this surprisingly compact island.

Grid is numbered streets and avenues crossing at right angles

In the areas above 14th Street, the city fathers imposed a strict grid upon Manhattan, leveling hills and tearing down existing homes to create straight, evenly spaced thoroughfares in all but a few places. The grid consists of numbered streets and avenues that cross each other at right angles. If you can count up to 100, you can get around this surprisingly compact island.

script_body: Travelers who need a break from the bustle of New York can escape to the Rubin, a serene museum of art from the Himalayas. Secular in origin — it was founded by an American millionaire and his wife who fell in love with the art of the region — its effect is nonetheless tremendously spiritual. The paintings, drawings, sculptures, and artifacts are all religious items, many used by traveling monks to teach Buddhism or to help worshippers deepen their meditation. That is why so many of the works are done on fabric: they were meant to be rolled up and carried. Many tell the stories of the various Buddhas, portraying meditating men with halos, snarling demons, teachers, and commoners in the deepest blues, ruby reds, emerald greens, and dazzling golds.

The cops who dispersed these groups of gaping men on 23rd Street would call out “23 skidoo!” — and so a slang term was born, meaning roughly “So long, sucker.”

script_body: At 28 acres, Hudson Yards is the largest private real estate development in American history — and amazingly, it was built in the most crowded city in the United States without displacing a single resident. The area it occupies, from 30th Street to 35th Street and Tenth Avenue to the river, covers the rail yards extending from Penn Station. An extraordinary feat of engineering created a platform above some 30 active railway tracks, with the massive skyscrapers resting partially on that platform and partially on caissons drilled into Manhattan's bedrock. The platform is wired with communication cables; rainwater from rooftops is filtered for on-site irrigation and drinking; and cooling units keep the heat of the train yards from affecting the 28,000 trees, grasses, wildflowers, and other plants in the park areas.

script_body: For all its state-of-the-art innovations, Hudson Yards is one of the most unpopular projects in recent New York memory. Many locals compare it unfavorably with Rockefeller Center, the city's last large-scale development and a place of unparalleled architectural harmony. Unlike that project, which had a team of architects and designers working in tandem, Hudson Yards is simply a cluster of unrelated skyscrapers created by half a dozen different firms. The often-sneaky use of public funds to underwrite this private luxury development has also been galling to many New Yorkers.

Designers inset a large triangle of glass in the floor for photo ops that look like you are floating thousands of feet above the ground, except for the faint scuff marks and shine on the glass. The walls around the deck are also glass, angled to afford glare-free views of the river and city.

script_body: The audacious arts complex The Shed is set on massive wheels that can be “nested” into the tower behind it, creating an open-air pavilion for outdoor performances. script_body: Pablo Picasso's Desmoiselles d'Avignon is a massive brothel scene in which Picasso experimented with a number of art styles — look closely and you'll see that one of the women's heads looks like an African mask, another profile is taken from Egyptian art, the woman in the middle assumes a classical Venus-like pose, and a leg of one of the figures devolves into cubist abstraction. Reportedly, Picasso painted the work when he was suffering from syphilis, which may be why the women appear so threatening.

script_body: MoMA doesn't rest on its laurels: in 2019, the museum closed for four months to “reimagine” itself. Pieces were re-hung and moved, and architectural re-finagling added 40,000 square feet of gallery space, expanding the museum by almost a third. The plan included new ground-level galleries that will always be free to the public, plus a performance studio and more elevators and escalators to combat gridlock. The Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, one of the city's most delightful spots to linger, was not touched.

script_body: Rise NY is an amusement park with the soul of a museum. Its marquee attraction is a ride that makes you feel like you're swooping over the city, set in a 40-foot-tall dome with 180-degree 3D videos and a soundtrack of every song ever written about the city. A faux subway ride barrels through time and space, from the debut of the subway up to Pizza Rat. A dozen galleries look at the many items invented in New York — the Singer sewing machine, the Otis elevator, the Broadway musical, hip hop — and how they made the city central to the industries they spawned.

script_body: Gotham's splendid “city within a city” was built in the 1930s at the height of the Depression. Thanks to the jobs it gave construction workers, it was the city's second-largest employer at the time, surpassed only by the federal Works Progress Administration. It remains a marvel of elegance and aspiration, a several-blocks-wide collection of 19 buildings that, despite their mass, create a space that is airy and light — a welcoming haven for both tourists and residents.

script_body: Adam Gopnik wrote about Times Square in The New Yorker, “No other part of New York has had such a melodramatic sensitivity to the changes in the city's history, with an image for every decade.” Think for a moment and the visions flood in: snazzy clubs and peroxide blonde chorus girls in the 1920s and '30s, sailors kissing girls at the end of World War II, the wisecracking small-time hoods of Guys and Dolls in the '50s, and the bleak urban decay of the '60s and '70s when, as Gopnik put it, “everything fell apart and Hell wafted up through the manhole covers.” Times Square is back on the upswing now, the porn shops banished and crime held mostly at bay.

script_body: Automaker Walter P. Chrysler commissioned architect William Van Alen to top them all, telling him he wanted a building “higher than the Eiffel Tower.” But the men behind the Bank of America had the same ambition, and hired Van Alen's former partner and sworn enemy, H. Craig Severance, to build the tallest building on the planet down on Wall Street. As each architect returned to the drafting board, Severance was sure he had won, completing the Bank of America building at 927 feet. Van Alen then unveiled the coup de grâce he'd been hiding in an elevator shaft — a silver spike to crown his building, making it, at 1,046 feet, an unbeatable 117 feet higher than his rival's.

script_body: There's no better introduction to New York than a visit to the Empire State Building. It's an apex of the New York skyline, both literally at 102 stories and 1,454 feet, and figuratively. From your bird's-eye perch you orient yourself geographically and see, with a clarity not possible on the ground, the miracle of Manhattan — that runt of an island that couldn't get much wider or longer, and so did what no other city before it had done and expanded to the skies, becoming a dense, pulsating city of boxy towers on a painfully narrow strip of land.

script_body: The Empire State Building opened in 1931 after just 14 months of construction, at a total cost of $25 million. It was the tallest building in the world from 1931 to 1970, when the World Trade Center took the title; it's still the 32nd tallest building on the planet. The oddly shaped spire at the top was meant to be a landing port for blimps, but high winds kept dirigibles from ever being able to anchor here.

script_body: In ancient Roman times, the entrances to great cities were framed with monumental arches meant to awe all who passed through. When Grand Central Terminal was built at the turn of the last century, its architects recognized that railroad terminals were the city's grand gateways, and filled them with the symbols of imperial Rome. On Grand Central's south facade, 10 colossal Doric fluted pillars tower over Park Avenue; above them, a massive statue of Mercury, the god of travel, spreads his arms in welcome as Hercules and Minerva, gods of strength and wisdom, lounge at his feet. The face of the clock below the sculpture is the largest piece of Tiffany glass in the world.

script_body: The Morgan contains examples of the written word from the beginning of recorded time — from pictorial Mesopotamian cylinder seals of the 4th millennium B.C., to papyrus rolls from ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome, to brilliantly colorful medieval illuminated manuscripts. Its crowning jewels are three editions of the Gutenberg Bible, the first book created using movable type. This is the only collection in the world to boast three editions; scholars come from around the globe to study them, as each is unique. Also in the collection are manuscripts by Mark Twain, Jane Austen, Charles Dickens, the Brontë sisters, Galileo, Bob Dylan, and James Joyce, one of 25 known surviving copies of the Declaration of Independence, and a First Folio of Shakespeare.

script_body: Can an observation deck be a work of art? That's the provocative question developer SL Green Realty posed when it hired artist Kenzo Digital to create an immersive experience atop its newest skyscraper. Set right on 42nd Street, Summit One has heart-of-the-action views like the Empire State Building's, with even better views of the Chrysler Building since it's just a few buildings over. Those views are amplified and fractured by mirrors covering most of this 1,750,212-square-foot space — and the floors are mirrored too. Other surprises include three fully transparent “sky boxes” jutting from the side of the building, letting brave visitors stare down 1,063 feet to the sidewalk, a room with floating mirrored orbs, and a digital screen that transposes visitors' faces onto clouds.

script_body: The Met was founded fairly late, conceived in 1870 by a group of wealthy businessmen and artists. A decade later Calvert Vaux, one of the architects of Central Park, was brought in to create the first red-brick building on this site — you can still see that facade, now the side wall of the European Sculpture Court. A little over a decade later an expansion was needed, so famed architect Richard Morris Hunt was tapped to create the majestic neoclassical Indiana-limestone edifice you see today, awing visitors who climb its mountain of steps and walk past its redwood-height pillars.

script_body: The Met is the giant among New York museums, figuratively and literally: at 1.6 million square feet it is not just the biggest museum in the city but the largest in the hemisphere — Frommer's argues it competes in stature with the Louvre, the Prado, the Uffizi, and the British Museum. Never a static institution, it now owns more than 3 million works of art spanning 5,000 years, across 18 curatorial departments — from Egyptian mummies to Greek statuary to Islamic carvings to Renaissance paintings to Native American masks.

source_passage: The giant among New York museums both figuratively and literally: At 1.6 million square feet, it’s not just the biggest museum in the city, it’s the largest one in this hemisphere. And I’d argue it competes in stature with the Louvre in Paris, the Prado in Madrid, the Uffizi in Florence, and the British Museum in London. Never a static institution, the museum and its collection have continued to grow, with the Met currently owning more than 3 million works of art spanning 5,000 years. You must choose carefully among the 18 curatorial departments and decide what interests you most. On view are masterworks from nearly all the world’s cultures—from Egyptian mummies to ancient Greek statuary to Islamic carvings to Renaissance paintings to Native American masks to 20th-century decorative arts.

script_body: On the second floor, the European paintings collection encompasses some 700 works. Its jewels include Velazquez's truer-than-life portrait of Juan de Pareja — the enslaved man whom the painter respected enough, as you can see in the painting, to set free; El Greco's brooding landscape of Toledo; 20 Rembrandts, among them Aristotle Contemplating the Bust of Homer, where Alexander the Great's pendant hangs from Aristotle's shirt; five light-kissed Vermeers; and a roomful of van Goghs.

script_body: The Egyptian Collection includes pieces discovered by the Met's own teams of archaeologists, such as miniature figures from a tomb in Thebes that show in intricate detail what daily life was like for a wealthy Egyptian. Its centerpiece is the Temple of Dendur, an actual temple to the goddess Isis dating to about 15 b.c. that was saved from the rising waters of the Nile after the construction of the Aswan Dam.

poi_name: Museum of the City of New York
script_body: Thanks to a 2016 overhaul, this century-old museum, founded in 1923, finally makes good on the promise of its name. It offers a textured, dramatic look at the improbable tale of a tiny, obscure Dutch colony that blossomed — and burned, and conned, and fought — into a world capital. Start in the basement, where a 30-minute film narrated by Stanley Tucci outlines the story, then move to the ground floor, where a gallery traces Gotham's history from Native American days through the 1900s, with electronic panels profiling New Yorkers from Alexander Hamilton to a murdered prostitute.

source_passage: Thanks to a 2016 overhaul, this century-old museum (founded in 1923) is finally making good on the promise of its name. Today, it offers visitors a textured, dramatic, suavely interactive look at the improbable tale of a tiny, obscure Dutch colony that blossomed—and burned, and conned, and fought—into a world capital. Start your visit in the basement, where an absorbing 30-minute film (narrated by Stanley Tucci) outlines the story. Next stop should be ground floor, where one gallery traces Gotham’s history from Native American days through the 1900s, displaying artifacts of all sorts, accompanied by electronic panels offering biographies of New Yorkers both well-known and obscure—everyone from Alexander Hamilton to a murdered prostitute—that illuminate different strands of the story.

script_body: New York is the city of the rectangle and the sharp right angle — our streets a grid, our buildings boxy and regular — until you get to the Guggenheim. Frank Lloyd Wright's delirious spiral of a museum sits among the towers of Fifth Avenue like a steroidal peacock among guinea hens. Critic Herbert Muschamp described it best: "What else but a building brought back from a dream would be windowless, have walls and floors that tilt and twist, begin on the top floor, and spiral in towards the center like an enigma?" Visiting this 1959 masterpiece and trudging up the ramps of its curving halls turns the standard museum experience into a profound journey — and sometimes a battle against vertigo.

script_body: Early critics dismissed the Guggenheim — Newsweek's insipid review was headlined "Museum or Cupcake?" — yet Frommer's argues even the most jaded visitor today feels the power of the place, the symbolic weight of infinite circle upon circle. And to answer the question nobody ever voices aloud: no, there have been no suicide jumps from over the low-slung rails, nor has anyone ever accidentally fallen to their death.

script_body: Since 1869 this institution has been both the country's preeminent private scientific research facility and its top museum for paleontology, zoology, anthropology, and now astronomy — and the flow between its research and curatorial sides keeps it fiercely vital. A few years ago scientists concluded that dinosaurs had not dragged their tails as long thought but waved them in the air as they walked. The curators responded by painstakingly dismantling the famed dino skeletons and reassembling them with tails erect, then placed one skeleton atop a section of a Texas riverbed where they had found fossilized dino footprints with no tail-dragging marks — a peephole into how scientific theories emerge.

Just a few years ago, for example, scientists concluded that dinosaurs had not dragged their tails as had long been thought but waved them in the air as they walked. The curators responded, painstakingly dismantling the museum’s famed dino skeletons and reassembling them with tails erect. Then, in a brilliant stroke, they placed one skeleton atop a section of a Texas riverbed where they had found fossilized dino footprints (sans tail-dragging marks), giving museumgoers a peephole into how scientific theories emerge.

script_body: In 2023 the $431-million Richard Gilder Center for Science, Education and Innovation opened, transforming the museum-going experience. Its new 230,000-square-foot structure houses 12% of the museum's collections, including an insectarium, a permanent butterfly vivarium, open storage exhibits, and a 360-degree Invisible Worlds Theater about the networks that underlie all life. Be sure to enter through this new center: the dazzling lobby mimics curving Southwestern American canyons, a sinuous look created by spraying structural concrete directly onto rebar.
