poi_name: Cathedral of St. John the Divine
script_body: Three odd facts make this a fascinating building. First: the largest cathedral in the world isn't St. Peter's in Rome — which is technically not a cathedral but a basilica — it's St. John the Divine in upper Manhattan. Second: despite the popish name, it isn't Catholic, it's Episcopalian. Third: though construction began in 1892, the building is still not complete, and many estimate it will take another 100 years to finish. The 121,000-square-foot structure blends Romanesque and Gothic elements, thanks to the varying tastes of the architects who worked on it over the past century. Most striking, it's being built without steel, in the classic Gothic manner — to that end, in 1979 a master stonecutter was brought from England to train Harlem youths in the art of traditional stonecutting. Much work remains, but what's in place is quite beautiful, especially the Rose Window in the apse, the largest in North America.

script_body: When you're NYC's oldest museum, founded in 1804, your attic gets mighty full. In past years that fourth-floor "attic" felt like a treasure hunt, its open storage units overflowing with telling artifacts — a Tiffany lamp here, a pair of historic pistols there, the plaster model head sculptor Daniel Chester French created for Washington's Lincoln Memorial in another corner. Then in 2017 the curators tidied up, replacing the open storage with three not-so-successful permanent galleries: a runway of too-many Tiffany lamps, a room of themed glass cases on facets of city life like "Childhood," "Fire," and "Collecting," and a center for women's history.

script_body: An offshoot of the Metropolitan Museum, the Cloisters is the only museum in the United States devoted wholly to medieval art, and it shows its masterworks in a setting that seems airlifted intact from some remote corner of the Pyrenees, or from a castle-lined town in Bavaria. Opened in 1934, the museum was in fact built in the United States, but 30% of its architectural elements — columns, pedestals, naves, doorframes, exquisite stained-glass windows — were salvaged from medieval European structures. It's a stunning mirage: even the land across the river was bought by patron John D. Rockefeller to thwart development and ensure the Cloisters' views would forever have a medieval face. At its heart are four cloisters, garden areas centered with a fountain and surrounded by covered walkways of the type seen in every monastery and abbey in Europe.

in a setting that seems to have been airlifted, utterly intact, from some
remote corner of the Pyrenees, or from a castle-lined town in Bavaria.
Opened in 1934, the museum was, in fact, built in the United States, but
30% of its architectural elements—columns, pedestals, naves, doorframes,
exquisite stained-glass windows—were salvaged from medieval European
structures. It’s a stunning mirage—even the land across the river was bought
by patron John D. Rockefeller to thwart development and ensure that the
Cloisters’ views would forever have a medieval face. At its heart are four
cloisters, garden areas centered with a fountain and surrounded by covered
walkways of the type seen in every monastery and abbey in Europe.

script_body: Pay special attention to the Unicorn Tapestries, one of only two full sets with a unicorn theme in the world — the other is in Paris. These richly detailed tapestries can be read on many levels: many scholars see the unicorn as a symbol of Christ, and the hunt to slay it as evocative of the Passion; others read the work as a metaphor for courtly love, with the hunt as courtship and the final tapestry — the unicorn trapped inside a wedding-ring-like fence — symbolizing marriage. Despite this captivity, the unicorn does look happy. They are an evocative slice of a past when nobles only hunted in packs of six, and unicorns were thought to be real — hence the long narwhal tooth in this room, which medieval people believed came from a unicorn.

script_body: The other must-see items are kept in the climate-controlled Campin Room — bring a sweater. There you'll find Robert de Campin's breakthrough Merode altarpiece, from around 1425, which placed the Annunciation — the moment an angel tells the Virgin Mary she will bear the child of God — in a secular setting rather than a church. It's also dramatic for its use of Jewish objects, including a prayer shawl and a vase with Hebrew-looking lettering, to establish Mary's background. Nearby is the so-called Cloisters Cross, one of only three known ivory crosses preserved from the 12th century — and the most complex, with over 90 figures and inscriptions painstakingly carved into the walrus-tusk ivory.

script_body: The Brooklyn Museum's Egyptian Collection, while not as extensive as the Met's, arguably has more masterpieces. When an ancient Egyptian piece comes up at auction, dealers often ask, 'Is it Brooklyn quality?' — the museum's collection being the benchmark for this sort of artifact. Among its wonders are a tiny 5,000-year-old, pre-dynastic terra cotta sculpture of a woman, nicknamed 'Birdwoman' for her beaklike face, and the Cartonnage of Nespanetjerenpere, a mummy case whose colors are electrically bright and unfaded.

Among the collection's many wonders are a tiny 5,000-year-old, pre-dynastic terra cotta sculpture of a woman, which curators have nicknamed “Birdwoman” for her beaklike face, one of very few intact sculptures from this long-ago era. Conditions aboard them were so atrocious that more than 11,500 Americans perished — more than the combined U.S. casualties in all the battles of the Revolution. Most of their bodies were simply dumped overboard into the water, making these waters the largest Revolutionary graveyard in the States.

script_body: The no. 7 train — which originates at Times Square and snakes mostly above ground through the heart of ethnic Queens — is popularly known as the International Express. Built by immigrants in the early 1900s, the no. 7 IRT brought those same immigrants to homes on the outer fringes of the city, and that tradition has continued as newcomers settle close by its elevated tracks. Get off in Sunnyside for Romanian groceries, in Jackson Heights for Indian saris and Sikh turbans, or ride to Flushing, where Queens's Chinatown is bigger than Manhattan's. In 1999 it was nominated as a National Millennium Trail and chosen to represent the American immigrant experience.

source_passage: The no. 7 train—which originates in Manhattan at Times Square, makes three stops in that borough, and then snakes, mostly above ground, through the heart of ethnic Queens—is also popularly known as the International Express. Built by immigrants in the early 1900s, the no. 7 IRT (Interborough Rapid Transit) brought those same immigrants to homes on the outer fringes of New York City. That tradition has continued as immigrants from around the world have settled close by the no. 7's elevated tracks. Get off in Sunnyside and see Romanian grocery stores and restaurants; a few stops farther in Jackson Heights, you'll see Indians in saris and Sikhs in turbans; go all the way to Flushing and you'll think you are in Chinatown. (You are—Queen's Chinatown is bigger than Manhattan's.) In 1999, the Queens Council on the Arts nominated the International Express for designation as a National Millennium Trail, and that resulted in its selection as representative of the American immigrant experience by the White House Millennium Council, the United States Department of Transportation, and the Rails-to-Trails Conservancy.

script_body: Manhattan’s 843-acre green oasis feels like nature, but very little here is natural. Every tree, every shrub, every lake, and most of the rolling hills were designed, planted, or blasted into existence by landscape architects Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux back in the 1850s. The two took a two-and-a-half-mile tract of swampland, farms, and suburban towns and created an Arcadia that bore no resemblance to what came before. Underneath the park, 95 miles of drainage pipes were laid to fill and periodically empty the four man-made lakes; at ground level the site was transformed with six million bricks, 65,000 cubic tons of gravel, 26,000 trees, and 250,000 shrubs. Even the dirt was imported — the natural topsoil was so poor that 500,000 cubic feet of it was shipped in from New Jersey. As Olmsted wrote, “Every foot of the park, every tree and bush, every arch, roadway and walk, has been fixed where it is with a purpose.”

These two geniuses took a 21⁄2-mile tract of swampland, farms, and suburban towns and created an Arcadia that had no resemblance whatever to what had come before. Underneath the park, 95 miles of drainage pipes were installed, many to fill and periodically empty the four lakes that were created; at ground level the site was transformed using six million bricks, 65,000 cubic tons of gravel, 26,000 trees, and 250,000 shrubs. script_body: The park’s purpose was nothing less than the health of the city — a place where New Yorkers could blow off steam and escape the stresses of urban life. Olmsted wanted more: a park that would be a bridge between classes. “There need to be places and time for re-unions,” he wrote, “[where] the rich and the poor, the cultivated and the self-made, shall be attracted together and encouraged to assimilate.” It didn’t happen at first — the park was too far from the homes of poor New Yorkers for them to visit — but that ideal was realized once the city itself wrapped around the park, finally making it a true central park.

Those who rallied for its creation felt that it was crucial to create a place where New Yorkers could blow off steam and get away from the stresses of urban life. Moreover, Olmsted wanted to create a park that would be a bridge between classes. “There need to be places and time for re-unions,” Olmsted wrote, “[where] the rich and the poor, the cultivated and the self-made, shall be attracted together and encouraged to assimilate.” Though that didn’t happen when the park was first finished—it was too far from the homes of poor New Yorkers for them to visit it—that ideal was realized when the city itself began to wrap around the park, making it finally a true central park.

script_body: As you stroll, you’ll cross three deliberately different kinds of landscape. There are pastoral vistas like the Sheep Meadow, meant to evoke a cultivated countryside; primitive portions where dense forestation shuts out any view of the city; and promenade zones, once used by the city’s aristocracy as an extension of their parlors — a place to strut and be seen. There’s no right way to see the park; you can ignore any highlight list and simply wander its curving paths for hidden nooks and surprise vistas.

script_body: This turreted castle is Olmsted and Vaux’s “folly” — a fantasy building — and it sits atop the second-highest elevation in the park. Inside is a nature observatory with good rainy-day activities for children. From Belvedere you also look down on the Great Lawn, which has gone through a number of incarnations: first a reservoir, then in the 1930s “Hooverville,” the shantytown where hundreds of homeless families lived out the Depression. Today it’s laid out in ballfields and often used as a concert space — Simon and Garfunkel famously reunited here in the 1980s in a widely televised concert.

script_body: This handsome obelisk was a gift to the United States from Egypt in 1881, in recognition of the help this country gave in building the Suez Canal. Transporting the 200-ton pillar took 38 days by ship from Alexandria to New York — and then another 144 days just to haul it from the Hudson River into Central Park. It originally stood at the Temple of the Sun in Heliopolis, believed to have been erected in 1600 b.c.; the Romans moved it in the 12th century to the front of a temple built by Cleopatra, which is how it got its name. A plaque at the base translates the hieroglyphics.

script_body: Bethesda Terrace is, without a doubt, the architectural heart of the park, and you’re likely to see a bride or two using this lovely area as a backdrop for wedding photographs. Approaching from the Mall, you’ll reach two massive posts on either side of the stairs, carved with symbols for day and night — the side with the witch on a broom is “night.” Look, too, at the carvings on the stairs down to the fountain: they represent the four seasons, and no two are alike.

script_body: At the southernmost tip of Manhattan, Battery Park has been growing kudzu-like for decades — it’s now a string of eclectic park spaces hugging the waterfront from just above the original Battery Park, where the Statue of Liberty ferry terminal sits, all the way up to Chambers Street, 21 acres in all. At the downtown-most end are stirring war monuments and the Seaglass Carousel, which dips and swoops riders around on massive plexiglass fish. Walking uptown you’ll find expansive lawns, a riverside promenade, terrific playgrounds, and a yacht marina.

At the downtown-most park are a number of stirring war monuments and the Seaglass Carousel (daily 10am–10pm; $6/ride), which dips and swoops riders around on massive plexiglass fish. It’s notable for its extensive programs of public concerts, movies, and even free juggling classes every good-weather day at noon. From roughly May through October the Sixth Avenue end becomes a stage for Broadway performers and free summer movies; in winter a small pond is set up for free ice-skating.

script_body: Who knew “adaptive reuse” could be this sexy? Domino Park sits on riverside property once owned by the Domino Sugar Refinery. In adapting the land, designer Lisa Switkin — of the firm behind the High Line — protected the landmarked refinery, making the hulking factory a spooky centerpiece, and reused other industrial artifacts to wonderful effect. That includes a gantry, a massive platform holding two cranes, painted the same turquoise that once lined the refinery’s walls; it’s now an elevated walkway with spectacular Manhattan views. In front of it sits a playground built to look like a mini-refinery, a volleyball court flanked by old syrup tanks, and a grove of metal corkscrews once used to stir syrup.

script_body: Situated a half-mile south of Manhattan, the 172-acre Governors Island was for many years a Coast Guard installation. Before that it was an army post for nearly 200 years and played a part in the Revolutionary War. In April 2010, New York City took it over. Because it had been a military base for so long, few New Yorkers — much less tourists — had ever visited. That has changed: much of the island is now a public park, with 22 acres designated a national monument centered around two 1812-era fortresses. In 2016, new parkland crowned by four man-made hills opened, giving visitors even more stellar views of Manhattan.

script_body: For years a secret, untamed garden hovered above the cityscape of Chelsea and Hell’s Kitchen. Formed from wild grass, flower, and weed seeds that randomly blew onto the tracks of a mile-and-a-half abandoned elevated railway, it became a hidden-in-plain-sight oasis for those New Yorkers brave and limber enough to scale the trestles. When the city began planning to tear down the historic rail structure — constructed 1929 to 1934 — a movement was born to save it and turn it into a grand public promenade with easy access from the street. Opened in 2009, it’s beautifully landscaped, in many places with the very “weeds” that once grew there, replanted where they wouldn’t crowd out the rest.

script_body: Gotham’s newest park seems to float like a watery mirage in the Hudson River. The engineering and architecture by Thomas Featherwick — the designer of Vessel — is stupendous: a set of 132 concrete “tulips,” all of differing heights, emerge from the water and join to form the base of the isle. On top of that Seuss-like structure are hills, amphitheaters, and eateries linked by winding paths and boulder scrambles. Landscaper Signe Nielson spared no expense, reportedly spending $5 million to cover the island with some 35 species of trees and 270 varieties of perennials, grasses, and bulbs, many chosen to attract bees and birds. It’s a gift to the city from media mogul Barry Diller, who spent $260 million on its construction.

The engineering and architecture by Thomas Featherwick (of Vessel; see p. 199) is stupendous, with a set of 132 concrete “tulips,” all of differing heights, emerging from the water and connecting to form the base of the isle. On top of that Seuss-like structure, hills were built, and amphitheaters, and eateries, all connected by a network of sinuously winding paths, stairs, and boulder scrambles. Landscaping superstar Signe Nielson was in charge of the greenery, and she spared no expense—it’s been reported she spent $5 million to cover the island with some 35 species of trees, 65 species of shrubs, and 270 varieties of perennials, grasses, vines, and bulbs. Many were chosen for their appeal to bees and birds, as it’s hoped this will be a sanctuary for those critters. It’s a gift to the city from media mogul Barry Diller, who spent $260 million for its construction and has pledged to supply money for its upkeep into the foreseeable future.

script_body: Also known as Jeffrey’s Hook Lighthouse, this historic beauty sits under the George Washington Bridge in Fort Washington Park, and it inspired the 1942 children’s classic The Little Red Lighthouse and the Great Gray Bridge by Hildegarde Swift and Lynd Ward. Built in New Jersey in 1880, it was reconstructed and moved to this spot in 1921 and stayed operational until 1947. It was slated for removal in 1951, but a public outcry over its popularity saved it; it’s now a New York City landmark and on the National Register of Historic Places.

script_body: Designed by Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux after their success with Central Park, this 562-acre expanse of woodland, meadows, and ponds is considered by many to be their masterpiece and the pièce de résistance of Brooklyn. The best approach is from Grand Army Plaza, presided over by the monumental Soldiers’ and Sailors’ Memorial Arch of 1892, honoring Union veterans. For the finest view of the lush landscape, follow the path to Meadowport Arch and on through to the Long Meadow, taking the loop around it — about an hour’s walk.

script_body: Prospect Park is studded with historic buildings. There’s the 1857 Italianate mansion Litchfield Villa on Prospect Park West; a 1906 Beaux Arts boathouse; a 1912 carousel whose white wooden horses were salvaged from a famous Coney Island merry-go-round; and the Lefferts Homestead Children’s Historic House Museum, a 1783 Dutch farmhouse with period furniture and kid-focused exhibits.

script_body: Another masterwork by Olmsted and Vaux, Riverside Park has always had one advantage over Central Park: glorious river views, which its garden-laced promenades make the most of. Among its monuments is Grant’s Tomb at 122nd Street, the largest mausoleum in the United States at 8,100 square feet. And the answer to that old riddle — who’s buried in Grant’s tomb? — is: no one. Ulysses S. Grant and his wife aren’t buried at all; their sarcophagi lie above ground.

script_body: This is the city’s funkiest green space, and it’s seen its share of political protest. In 1988, a standoff between the police and the homeless people living here culminated in five days of rioting and charges of police brutality. Incorporated as a park in 1878, Tompkins Square once had a band shell where an early version of the Grateful Dead made their East Coast debut, though that has since been torn down.

script_body: Union Square Park’s tradition of political activism goes back to the very first Labor Day Parade in 1882, which ended right here. Ever since, it’s been soapbox central — a place where orators come daily to blast whatever administration is in power and weigh in on the big topics of the day. A statue of Gandhi, a gift of the Indian people, calmly watches over the proceedings, a fresh wreath of flowers always draped about his neck.

script_body: This park is nothing if not tuneful: it has long been a gathering place for amateur musicians, who lug their instruments here for impromptu concerts each weekend and many fine-weather weeknights. The round fountain in the center serves as a stage for a dozen or so regular comedians, acrobats, and dancers good enough to draw crowds of a hundred people or more. And on the park’s southwest corner, intense chess matches run from noon to sundown — the regulars are real sharks.

script_body: Lincoln Center is a giant complex of theaters on the west side of Manhattan, flanking Columbus Avenue between 62nd and 65th streets. It hosts everything from major symphonic premieres to the Big Apple Circus, but it's most famous for its presentation of classic works of music, dance, opera, film, and theater. Toward that end it houses a number of permanent companies and plays host to the world's leading performing arts organizations.

script_body: Behind these walls live some of the most storied names in American performing arts. The resident companies include the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center, the Film Society of Lincoln Center, and Lincoln Center Theater — the last of which houses both a well-respected Broadway theater and an off-Broadway theater. Among the center's other residents are the Metropolitan Opera, the New York City Ballet, the Juilliard School, the New York Philharmonic, and the American Ballet Theatre.

script_body: Here's the lovely little secret about this house: the cheap seats get the best sound. Sit in the pricey orchestra section and you may have trouble making out the words, but buy a “family circle” seat way up high and the voices will float up to you in all their crystalline clarity. One warning, though — don't show up late. The Met does not seat latecomers; arrive after the curtain and you'll watch the first act on a video screen in the basement.

script_body: The blockbuster modern dance shows tend to play the Joyce, and it's not hard to see why — it's simply the best space in the city to see dance, with not a bad seat in the house. script_body: The New York City Ballet was founded by Lincoln Kirstein and the twentieth century's greatest ballet choreographer, George Balanchine. Balanchine's version of The Nutcracker is a holiday classic and one of the most difficult tickets to get each Christmas season.

script_body: BAM is more than one room. Along with the large BAM Opera House and the smaller BAM Harvey Theater, the organization runs a dedicated movie theater — the BAM Rose Cinema — for art films, and a cafe space where up-and-coming talent perform.

script_body: This small theater, just 125 seats, is set on an actual barge moored near the Brooklyn Bridge, with big views of the Manhattan skyline and acoustics to die for. Pianissimos are more piano here and fortissimos molto-loud, even when played by a solo piano or string quartet. It's one of the few truly intimate stages in the city, and the prices are intimate too, starting at just $35.

source_passage: Bargemusic         This small theater (125 seats), set on an actual barge moored near the Brooklyn Bridge, has big views of the Manhattan skyline and acoustics to die for. Pianissimos are more piano here and fortissimos molto-loud, even when played by a solo piano or string quartet. This is one of the few truly intimate stages in the city, and the prices are intimate, too, starting at just $35 a pop ($30 seniors, $20 kids and students, cash only). At Fulton Ferry Landing (just south of the Brooklyn Bridge), Brooklyn.

script_body: This colossal former military space, with a 55,000-square-foot drill hall at its core, has made a name for itself in recent years for the prestige, scope — often huge — and quirkiness of the shows it has produced and brought in from all corners of the globe. They've included Robert Icke's Olivier Award-winning production The Doctor with Juliet Stevenson, several large pieces by the doyenne of French theater Ariane Mnouchkine, and new dance works by Anne Teresa de Keersmaeker.

source_passage: Park Avenue Armory              This colossal former military space, with a 55,000-square-foot drill hall at its core, has made a name for itself in recent years for the prestige, scope (often huuuge), and quirkiness of the shows it has produced and/or brought in from all corners of the globe. They’ve included director Robert Icke’s Olivier Award–winning production The Doctor (with Juliet Stevenson), several large pieces by the doyenne of French theater Ariane Mnouchkine, new dance works by Anne Teresa de Keersmaeker, and dozens of musical recitals.

script_body: It's hard to classify just what Joe's Pub is, beyond a very handsome space in a landmark building that hosts performances and serves strong cocktails and pub food. Its show roster is all over the map — spoken-word artists, rising singer/songwriters, jazz bands, pop stars, you name it. Past performers include Alicia Keys, fashion designer Isaac Mizrahi, Patti LuPone, and Wynton Marsalis.
